rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imruʾ al-Qays’s expressions show that the construction denotes a person’s complete inability to do something, even to fight.
rows.anchor: meaning “such and such a person has no not the slightest ability to do anything”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The real blow at Badr came from angels as they claimed the disbelievers’ souls; seeing it would show their total rout.
rows.anchor: the real beating the disbelievers were inflicted with in the battle of Badr was from the angels when they claimed their souls

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the angelic punishment comes Hell’s punishment, which cannot be imagined in this world.
rows.anchor: After that is the phase of the punishment of Hell that cannot be even be imagined in this world.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The punished reap what they sow, while God does not wrong His servants.
rows.anchor: this is the punishment of your own misdeeds and God does not do the slightest of injustice to His servants

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term for Pharaoh’s house extends beyond children to followers and the nation.
rows.anchor: children but also to one’s followers and nation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s nation and earlier peoples suffered because of ingratitude, denial of God’s revelations, and failure to value His signs.
rows.anchor: The fate of the Pharaoh’s nation and those before them was because of their ingratitude, denying God’s revelations and not duly valuing His signs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s seizure of nations for sin is a warning punishment, especially manifested after a messenger is sent.
rows.anchor: the punishment referred to in the words “so, God seized them for their sins” is the one God inflicts on nations to warn them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier examples of this established divine practice are cited in al-Baqarah, al-Anʿām, and al-Aʿrāf.
rows.anchor: to understand this established practice of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Badr reversal was meant to jolt Quraysh as a warning; earlier nations are examples, and their response to it remains to be seen.
rows.anchor: this reversal suffered by the Quraysh in the battle of Badr was meant to shake and jolt them and was in accordance with God’s established practice

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Quraysh persist in denying their messenger and God’s revelations, God will destroy them like Pharaoh’s nation and earlier peoples.
rows.anchor: If they become adamant on their denial, God will destroy them the way he destroyed the Pharaoh’s nation and others.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The twice-occurring reference is not redundant: one occurrence recalls the warning to earlier nations, the other threatens decisive punishment if it is ignored.
rows.anchor: This is not a repetition; in fact, two different things are stated at both places.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A nation receives God’s favor because of certain traits and loses it when it abandons them; its deviance brings warning and conclusive communication, and it bears responsibility if the favor is removed.
rows.anchor: When God does a favour to a nation, it is not without reason. It is because it professes certain attributes and traits.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh still have a chance to benefit: God does not forcibly take their favor, and their wayward beliefs and deeds are causing their danger.
rows.anchor: the Quraysh are admonished that they still have a chance and they can avail it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s hearing and knowledge ground a law under which He observes how nations use the authority, means, and resources He grants them.
rows.anchor: After granting authority, means and resources to nations, He continues to observe what they do on the basis of these attributes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Quraysh do not learn from the warnings, they will face the decisive punishment suffered by Pharaoh’s people.
rows.anchor: The words “they face the same as happened with the people of the Pharaoh” depict the fate the Quraysh will meet in the future

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses’ wording differs: the first speaks of denying God’s signs and being seized for sins, while the second speaks of rejecting their Lord’s signs and being destroyed for sins.
rows.anchor: The difference of words and tone found in both these verses may be noted.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage refers to Jews and other post-migration treaty partners, including Juhaynah, Ḍamrah, and Banū Mudlij; the Prophet kept the agreements, while they broke them under Jewish or Quraysh provocation or pressure.
rows.anchor: They include the tribes of Juhaynah, Ḍamrah and the Banū Mudlij among others.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic description, also explained at 8:22, denies these people the purpose and value of existence because they cannot think or understand; they will not believe and no longer benefit the world.
rows.anchor: It negates the very reason for their existence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A messenger is the final means of communicating truth conclusively; those who remain blind after him have no cure, and human life is for reflection and reform.
rows.anchor: a messenger is the final means of conclusive communication of the truth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The treaty-breakers repeatedly sought to harm believers when tested and remained sympathetic to Quraysh, showing hardheartedness, shallow character, and lack of honor.
rows.anchor: Whenever a testing situation would arise, they would try to harm the believers. Their sympathies continued to be with the Quraysh.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “At every instance” means they would break the treaty whenever a comparable test arose.
rows.anchor: for the purpose for which this treaty was made, if a similar trial would befall, they would never abide by it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Have no fear” means they would not refrain from treaty-breaking or its consequences; keeping promises is a universal norm and accountability before God.
rows.anchor: abiding by promises is a universally accepted norm and also a matter of accountability before God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their present nuisance is hidden and they lack courage to act openly, but if fought they should be struck hard enough to rout combatants and deter those planning similar actions.
rows.anchor: strike them in such a way that you also rout those behind them so that they may learn a lesson.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Treaty duties are mutual, and equal-term retaliation must be proportionate to the harm inflicted.
rows.anchor: the revenge should never exceed the harm inflicted: it should be commensurate with it

rows.speaker: some people
rows.claim: Some derive from the equal-terms expression a duty to inform the other party when terminating a treaty.
rows.anchor: Some people have derived from this expression that it is essential to inform the opposite party about the termination of a treaty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author finds no argument in this expression for the view that treaty termination must be announced to the other party.
rows.anchor: I could find no argument for this deduction in it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hypothetical fear alone cannot end a treaty; the emphatic wording and equal-terms condition indicate that the other side must actually breach it.
rows.anchor: a mere hypothetical fear is not enough to end a treaty. The other party must have practically breached it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s dislike of treachery declares His disavowal of traitors; believers who maintain relations with them should recognize they are close with people God hates.
rows.anchor: God has no relation with such treacherous people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next passage commands war preparation because Quraysh were enraged after Badr and the Jews were plotting defeat after their earlier reliance on Quraysh failed.
rows.anchor: after being defeated in the battle of Badr, the Quraysh were writhing with anger.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet may make peace if the enemy genuinely compromises, but should remember God’s help if they use compromise as a trick.
rows.anchor: if the enemy shows any compromising attitude, he too can make peace with them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should not fear the believers’ small number: God and the believers suffice, ten can face a hundred, heart-strength matters more than numbers, and the enemy’s hearts are hollow.
rows.anchor: ten of them will be enough for a hundred disbelievers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Concomitant indications place 8:66 after the believers grew numerous; it lightened the previous verse’s burden and follows it because it shares its topic.
rows.anchor: verse 66, the last verse of this section, was revealed when the believers had become large in number.

none: translation of verses only; no commentary to record
